abstract: The vomeronasal system consists of a vomeronasal organ (VNO) and an accessory olfactory bulb (AOB) that act together to detect specific substances such as pheromones. The degree to which this system has developed varies among carnivorans. Raccoon dogs (Nyctereutes viverrinus) communicate using feces and urine, suggesting a significant role of the vomeronasal system. Here, we histologically detail the VNO and AOB of raccoon dogs. The VNO had a J-shaped cartilage and opened anteriorly into the incisive duct. Numerous blood vessels surrounded the vomeronasal lumen, which was medially lined by sensory epithelium. The VNO contained secretory vomeronasal glands in the submucosa, multicellular intraepithelial glands in non-sensory epithelium, and goblet cells. Submucosal glands were periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) positive and negative for Alcian blue (pH 2.5). Multicellular intraepithelial glands positive for PAS were observed in three of the six raccoon dogs analyzed herein; the glands were AB-negative and positive in one and two, respectively. The vomeronasal nerve and glomerular layers were histologically distinguishable in the AOB, but deeper layers comprised a single plexiform-granule layer with intermingled mitral/tufted and granular cells. These characteristics of raccoon dog AOBs resembled those of domesticated dogs rather than wild red foxes and gray wolves. The vomeronasal nerve and glomerular layers were positive for anti-Gαi2 and negative for anti-Gαo, suggesting that vomeronasal type 1 receptors are functionally expressed in the vomeronasal system of raccoon dogs. Overall, our findings morphologically indicated that raccoon dogs communicate using the vomeronasal system.
title: The vomeronasal system of the Japanese raccoon dog, Nyctereutes viverrinus

abstract: Abstract Aggression and courtship are widely studied social behaviors in Drosophila melanogaster , but their accurate quantification remains a practical obstacle. Manual scoring of these behaviors is time consuming, prone to inter‐observer variability, and difficult to scale, while existing automated tools often require expensive hardware or specialized skills. This article provides step‐by‐step protocols for implementing DANCE ( Drosophila Aggression and Courtship Evaluator), a low‐cost platform that combines supervised machine learning classifiers with recording hardware built from repurposed medicine blister packs, acrylic sheets, and consumer smartphones. The protocols describe how to construct the aggression and courtship arenas, acquire standardized videos using a smartphone over a tablet backlight, and process recordings through an automated pipeline that tracks individual flies in FlyTracker and scores behavior using six pretrained JAABA classifiers, one for aggressive lunges and five for the stages of male courtship. Additional protocols describe how to train new classifiers, validate classifier performance against manual annotation, and add an optogenetic stimulation module. Each protocol specifies the required materials, software versions, parameter settings, and expected outputs, so that a user with no prior experience in automated behavioral analysis can generate per‐dyad behavioral measurements suitable for statistical comparison. All classifiers, analysis scripts, and worked examples are available at https://github.com/agrawallab/DANCE . The platform was originally described and validated by Yadav et al. title: DANCE: Step‐by‐Step Protocol for Automated Quantification of Drosophila Aggression and Courtship

abstract: Song amplitude is an important but comparatively understudied dimension of avian acoustic communication, influencing signal transmission, detectability and social interactions. We investigated ecological and structural drivers of song amplitude variation in six passerine species using 3265 songs recorded from 120 territorial males. Body size was associated with cross-species variation in amplitude only when the largest and loudest species, the Great Reed Warbler, was included. Across species, song amplitude declined with increasing temperature, relative humidity and time after sunrise, whereas ambient noise showed no evidence of a generalised Lombard effect. Song rate, song length and peak frequency were consistent predictors of amplitude, with peak frequency showing the strongest association. Within-species analyses revealed substantial heterogeneity in environmental effects, whereas relationships between amplitude and song structure were more consistent across species. Individual identity explained considerable variation in amplitude, indicating pronounced within-species variability in vocal output. Overall, our results suggest that song amplitude is a flexible component of vocal performance shaped primarily by song structure and signalling context rather than by body size alone. These findings emphasise the importance of considering both behavioural and ecological sources of variation when interpreting patterns of acoustic signalling in birds.
title: Ecological and Structural Drivers of Song Amplitude Variation in Passerines

abstract: Animals possess various defensive strategies to avoid predation (Endler, 1991; Ruxton et al., 2018; Sugiura, 2020). Defenses that act before predator contact are defined as primary defenses, whereas those that function after contact are defined as secondary defenses (Ruxton et al., 2018). Among primary defenses, masquerade—where prey resembles a twig, leaf, pebble, or bird dropping—enables prey to avoid predation by being misclassified as an inedible object, even after detection (Skelhorn, 2015). However, masquerading prey may face increased predation risk when they move for feeding or reproduction, as the effectiveness of their masquerade declines (Yin et al., 2015). Such prey may therefore possess secondary defenses in addition to masquerade. Despite this possibility, little attention has been paid to how masquerading species defend themselves after their masquerade fails. Adults of the weevil Sternuchopsis trifida (Coleoptera: Curculionidae) are commonly found on the leaves and stems of the kudzu vine, Pueraria lobata (Fabaceae), in Japan (Figure 1a,b; Appendix S1: Table S1). When resting on leaves, their contrasting white-and-black body coloration appears conspicuous against the green background, resembling a bird dropping when viewed from a distance (Figure 1c,d). Such bird-dropping-like coloration, which occurs in various arthropods, is known to function as masquerade to avoid predation (Liu et al., 2014; Skelhorn, 2015). On days in May and June 2025, we observed many adults actively moving on kudzu plants at a grassland site in Hyogo, central Japan, a behavior likely to increase their risk of recognition as prey by predators such as frogs, which respond to movement. At the same site during the same season, the Japanese tree frog Dryophytes japonicus (Anura: Hylidae) was also found on kudzu (Figure 1e). Adult D. japonicus are known to prey on a wide variety of arthropods, including adult weevils (Hirai & Matsui, 2000; Sano & Shinohara, 2012). This species forages both during the day and at night (Hirai & Matsui, 2000; Taniguchi et al., 2005) and has been observed to attack diurnal insects in daylight (Matsubara & Sugiura, 2017). Therefore, D. japonicus potentially attacks moving adult S. trifida on kudzu leaves. To investigate how adult weevils can defend against tree frogs, we presented adult S. trifida (body length: 8.5–9.6 mm; body mass: 69.4–107.8 mg) to adult D. japonicus (snout–vent length: 27.4–33.4 mm; mass: 1.9–3.5 g) under laboratory conditions at 25°C (see Appendix S1: Materials and Methods, Table S2). All tree frogs (N = 20) reacted to weevil movements and attacked them. However, only two frogs (10%) successfully swallowed them (Figure 2). Six frogs rejected the weevils immediately after their tongues contacted them. Thirteen frogs had their tongues or lips grasped by weevils (Figure 1f), and 12 of these (92%) failed to swallow them (Figure 2; Video S1). During grasping, weevils did not appear to use their sharp tarsal claws. Instead, adult S. trifida possess inward-facing tibial and femoral spines (Appendix S1: Figure S1; Morimoto, 1984) that were observed to cling to the frog's tongue or mouthparts, likely helping them maintain a firm hold on the predator. In the 11 frogs whose tongues were firmly grasped (Figure 1f), frogs required 3–73 min (median: 14 min) to dislodge the weevils. To test whether grasping behavior is essential for successful defense against tree frogs, we provided adult D. japonicus (26.2–34.5 mm; 1.7–3.5 g) with adult S. trifida (8.1–9.8 mm; 57.2–104.9 mg) whose legs had been amputated at the mid-femur (thigh segment) with scissors (Appendix S1: Materials and Methods, Table S2). All tree frogs attacked the treated weevils, and none of the treated weevils were able to grasp the frogs. Of the 20 tree frogs, nine (45%) successfully swallowed the treated weevils (Figure 2). Other frogs rejected the weevils immediately after their tongues contacted them. Leg amputation increased the predation rate by tree frogs from 10% to 45% (Figure 2). A generalized linear model (GLM) analysis revealed a significant effect of leg removal (Appendix S1: Table S3). Therefore, adult S. trifida possess an effective secondary defensive strategy, in which they grasp the frog's tongue or lip with their legs to prevent swallowing. To investigate whether adult S. trifida can successfully defend against another frog species, we presented adult S. trifida (8.2–9.7 mm; 63.7–111.0 mg) to the black-spotted pond frog Pelophylax nigromaculatus (Anura: Ranidae) (36.4–78.4 mm; 4.1–50.0 g), which is larger than tree frogs. All pond frogs (N = 20) attacked the weevils, and 90% successfully swallowed them (Figure 2). Sixteen pond frogs consumed the weevils without being grasped by their legs. While four were grasped, two of these consumed the weevils. When leg-amputated weevils were presented, 95% of the 20 pond frogs successfully swallowed them (Figure 2). A GLM analysis showed no significant difference in predation rate between the control and leg-removal treatments (Appendix S1: Table S4). Only a few adult S. trifida managed to grasp the tongue or lip of pond frogs, suggesting that grasping defenses are not effective against larger frog species. Grasping behavior has been reported as a defensive response in which animals cling firmly to a substrate to prevent capture or ingestion by predators (Borne et al., 2021; Eisner & Aneshansley, 2000). Adult S. trifida are also observed clinging tightly to kudzu stems (Figure 1b), suggesting that this behavior may serve a similar function. In contrast, the grasping observed in the present study represents a previously undocumented defensive strategy, in which the prey holds onto the predator itself rather than onto the substrate (Figure 1f). Even when the legs were amputated, 55% of attacks by tree frogs resulted in rejection of adult S. trifida (Figure 2). This suggests that additional defenses other than grasping contribute to rejection. First, adult S. trifida possess a long and rigid rostrum (Figure 1a), which sometimes contacts the frog's tongue or mouthparts during attacks. Because the rostrum projects forward as a stiff, elongated structure, it can press against the inner surfaces of the frog's mouth when the prey is being transported toward the esophagus. Such contact may mechanically interfere with prey handling, making it difficult for the frog to reposition the prey for swallowing and thereby increasing the likelihood of rejection. Second, some tree frogs may have responded to chemical cues from adult S. trifida, as frogs can detect chemicals using their tongues (Matsubara & Sugiura, 2017). Although no glands or defensive chemical secretions have been detected in adult S. trifida, leg amputation occasionally caused a small amount of hemolymph to exude from the cut surface. Other morphological or behavioral traits might also play a role in rejection. Determining the relative importance of these potential factors will require further analyses, such as chemical profiling of the hemolymph or behavioral assays manipulating the rostrum. The movement of prey profoundly affects how their visual signals are perceived by predators (Cuthill et al., 2019). In masquerading species, such movement can either disrupt or preserve misclassification by predators, depending on the ecological context (Hall et al., 2017; Yin et al., 2015). In S. trifida, movement increases the likelihood of being recognized as prey, because the species is solitary, occurs on visually contrasting backgrounds, and mimics a non-moving model. We observed that adult S. trifida were attacked by tree frogs but avoided being swallowed by clinging tightly to the frog's tongue or lip (Figure 1f; Video S1). Their grip was so strong that the frogs required considerable time to dislodge them. Such handling difficulty may cause frogs to associate the weevil's conspicuous coloration with an unpleasant experience, thereby discouraging future attacks. We therefore hypothesize that the white-and-black coloration of S. trifida functions as masquerade when stationary, but in combination with strong secondary defenses, acts as aposematism when the insect is moving. A dual function of body coloration has been reported in some insects (Barnett & Cuthill, 2014; Kikuchi et al., 2017; Tullberg et al., 2005), with one example being the coexistence of camouflage and aposematism—blending into the background at a distance but becoming conspicuous at close range (Tullberg et al., 2005). However, few previous studies have focused on the defensive role of bird-dropping-like coloration as aposematism. To test this hypothesis, behavioral experiments are required to determine whether predators that have experienced weevil defenses subsequently avoid individuals with this coloration. title: Beyond masquerade: Grasping the predator prevents swallowing in a bird‐dropping‐like weevil

abstract: Birdsong, as many complex behavioral patterns, needs to be acquired, maintained and adjusted throughout life. In songbirds, these tasks are held by a specialized neural network, the song control system. Nightly sleep has been shown to be highly relevant for the song learning and maintenance process. Distinct diurnal changes in neuronal activity can be observed in several song control areas expressing melatonin receptors, frequently in inhibitory interneurons. By disentangling the effect of melatonin from the confounding effects of sleep while continuously monitoring the activity of individual neurons in the song control system of freely moving adult male zebra finches for several days, we show a direct effect of melatonin on spontaneous as well as auditory evoked activity of song control neurons. We therefore suggest melatonin as an endocrine switch that enables night-time neural functions of song control neurons, crucial for formation and consolidation of song motor memory.
title: Nightly changes in neural activity and auditory processing of song control neurons depend on melatonin

abstract: In arid environments or during prolonged drought periods, maintaining hydration becomes increasingly challenging, often requiring organisms to reduce investment in costly behaviors. Vocal performance is sensitive to hydration status because systemic dehydration can alter vocal fold mechanics and reduce vocal efficiency. In many mammals, vocalizations are produced when expiratory airflow induces self-sustained vibration of the vocal folds, making this mechanism vulnerable to systemic water imbalance. This study tested whether dehydration alters singing rate and acoustic song parameters in adult California mice (Peromyscus californicus). Mice were recorded over three days of water deprivation. Baseline variation was first assessed in a control group of ten animals with unrestricted water access; vocal activity and seven acoustic parameters showed no consistent daily trends. Vocal activity and acoustic parameters were then evaluated in 14 mice subjected to 72 h of water deprivation. Vocal activity did not decline during dehydration. Fundamental frequency, sound intensity, and syllable repetition rate decreased significantly during late-stage dehydration but recovered toward baseline after water restoration. Changes in fundamental frequency and sound intensity are consistent with altered vocal fold biomechanics associated with reduced tissue hydration, whereas reduced syllable repetition rate without changes in syllable duration suggests an additional effect on temporal control of vocal output. These findings demonstrate that systemic dehydration affects multiple components of vocal production and that vocal performance recovers following rehydration.
title: Water limitation modifies vocal performance in California mice: implications for acoustic communication under environmental stress

abstract: Goal-directed intentionality is the ability to communicate with the intention of eliciting reactions from recipients. Long considered uniquely human, today it has been reported in the signalling of several species, most notably in the large, flexible gestural repertoires of non-human apes. Semi-captive elephants have also shown goal-directed intentionality when gesturing to humans. However, whether wild elephants gesture intentionally to conspecifics has not been systematically explored. Elephants frequently engage in agonistic interactions, in which goal-directed intentional communication may help resolve conflict and prevent escalation. Here, we systematically investigated intentional gesturing in wild African savannah elephants by examining agonistic interactions in the Addo and Marakele populations in South Africa. Elephants used 41 gesture types (derived from 32 gesture actions) to communicate two main goals: "Move away" and "Stop behaviour". The gesture types used by the populations largely overlapped, suggesting a shared context-specific repertoire for agonistic interactions. However, the populations differed in the gesture types they used most frequently and in the resources they competed over (water in Addo, reeds in Marakele). Our study supports the convergent evolution of extensive and flexible intentional gestural communication in elephants, providing insights into the drivers of elephant agonistic behaviour and highlighting potential conservation implications.
title: Elephant gestural communication during agonistic interactions: repertoire, intentionality, and goals

abstract: Scalp-recorded auditory evoked potentials (AEPs) allow the same non-invasive metrics used in human auditory neuroscience to be applied to non-human primates, yet the basic acoustic response properties of AEPs in the common marmoset (Callithrix jacchus) remain poorly characterized. We recorded AEPs from two awake marmosets in response to pure tones spanning eight frequencies (125-16,000 Hz) and three intensities (45-75 dB SPL), and quantified response magnitude as the global field power of five AEP components (P1, N1, P2, N2, and the late negativity, LN). AEP magnitude depended strongly on stimulus frequency, peaking at 1000 Hz for every component and animal and declining at both lower and higher frequencies. AEP magnitude also increased with intensity, and the two factors interacted for most components, with frequency tuning becoming more pronounced at higher intensities. We further compared three reference montages and found that reference choice strongly altered scalp polarity: the canonical positive-negative-positive P1-N1-P2 sequence was preserved with linked earlobes, whereas common median and common average references produced polarity reversals between frontal and parieto-occipital sites. These data suggest that marmoset AEPs carry a frequency dependence and a reference-dependent polarity that must be controlled when designing and interpreting more complex auditory paradigms such as oddball and mismatch negativity designs in this species.
title: Frequency, intensity, and reference dependence of scalp-recorded auditory evoked potentials in the common marmoset

abstract: Passive acoustic monitoring (PAM) constitutes an effective means to monitor the status of coastal marine environments. Here, acoustic data were collected over a three-month period using an autonomous underwater recorder deployed in Xiamen Bay, Southeast China, during the construction of a new airport. Customized scripts based on power spectral density (PSD) and band-integrated sound pressure levels (SPLs) analysis were used to examine the local underwater ambient noise, which was found to be dominated by sounds below 10 kHz. SPLs were positively correlated with wind speed across the Bands I-III (1/3-octave bands centered between 50 Hz and 20 kHz). Clear diel patterns were observed mainly below 2.5 kHz, whereas variations at higher frequencies were less than 2.4 dB re 1 μPa throughout the day. Shrimp snaps and vessel noise were determined as likely primary contributors to the low-frequency acoustic energy. Clicks of Indo-Pacific humpback dolphins (Sousa chinensis) constituted the key factor to impact acoustic energy above 50 kHz but were infrequent and short in duration, contributing little to the overall acoustic baseline. This study provides a short-term construction-phase acoustic baseline, serving as an initial reference for future long-term monitoring networks and comparisons with the operational phase of the airport.
title: Examination of a short-term underwater soundscape in a southeast Chinese Bay

abstract: Anthropogenic underwater noise is an increasing concern in marine environments, yet physiological responses of sea turtles remain poorly understood. We examined cardiac responses to underwater sound playback in three juvenile green turtles (Chelonia mydas) and four juvenile loggerhead turtles (Caretta caretta) maintained after incidental capture. Electrocardiogram, acceleration, depth, and turtle-borne acoustic data were recorded during 44 trials. Green turtles showed prolongation of the RR interval (the time between successive heartbeats) on average after playback, particularly under vessel noise, whereas loggerhead turtles showed RR interval shortening. Generalized estimating equation models showed contrasting vessel-control response patterns between the two datasets. These patterns remained after accounting for mean changes in activity or depth, suggesting that responses were not explained solely by broad-scale movement or vertical displacement. Interpretation is limited by small sample size, differing experimental settings, variable playback durations, and estimated rather than directly measured sound pressure levels. Cardiac biologging can reveal physiological responses to underwater sound.
title: Cardiac responses to underwater sound playback in juvenile green and loggerhead sea turtles: an exploratory biologging study

abstract: Billions of birds migrate annually, triggered by endogenous behaviors but also by ecoclimatic drivers which are shifting with climate change. These dynamics play out over huge spatiotemporal scales, making monitoring of phenology challenging with traditional biodiversity survey approaches. In this study, over a complete spring migration season (April through June), we collected 37,429 hours of audio from 28 networked sensors in forests across Norway using a nationwide passive acoustic monitoring (PAM) system. We applied an open-source detection algorithm to automatically classify bird vocalizations; through expert validation we found the algorithm classified 57 species (14 full migrants) with at least 80% precision. Using these automated detections, we developed regional arrival curves for three common migratory passerines: Willow Warbler, Common Chiffchaff, and Spotted Flycatcher. We then demonstrate that PAM detections can be used to train audio species distribution models that map how species vocalization probability changes across Norway during spring migration. Lastly, we discuss how PAM can complement existing manual surveys to support the design and implementation of effective policy and conservation measures.
title: National-scale acoustic monitoring of avian biodiversity and migration

abstract: Cavitation in fluid machinery degrades hydrodynamic performance and generates severe vibration and noise. Inspired by humpback whale pectoral flipper tubercles, this study proposes a bionic groove–nodule leading-edge structure for the NACA0009 hydrofoil to synergistically suppress cavitation and radiated noise. A steady-state RANS simulation based on the Shear Stress Transport k–ω model provides the initial flow field, followed by large eddy simulation (LES) coupled with the Schnerr–Sauer cavitation model to resolve the unsteady cavitating flow. All results are derived from the transient LES data at an angle of attack of 10° and cavitation number σ = 1.07, corresponding to the optimal design point from a preliminary parametric screening. The bionic structure modifies the pressure distribution and delays suction-surface flow separation, achieving up to 66% reduction in vapor volume. The groove–nodule leading edge disrupts sheet cavitation into complex three-dimensional vortex systems, fragmenting large-scale vortical structures into smaller dissipative clusters. This reduces surface dipole source strength and, as inferred from coherence analysis, relatively increases quadrupole source contributions with lower radiation efficiency. Within the 300–600 Hz critical band, the bionic hydrofoil achieves an average far-field sound pressure level (SPL) reduction of 10.2 dB, with a peak overall SPL decrease in 7.07 dB. Coherence analysis confirms a 21.6% reduction in flow–acoustic coupling strength across the entire frequency band. This study demonstrates the dual efficacy of the bionic design in simultaneously suppressing cavitation and broadband noise, offering biomimetic insights for high-performance, low-noise hydraulic blades.
title: Study of cavitation and noise characteristics of hydrofoil with bionic groove–nodule leading edge structure

abstract: Aerodynamic noise generated in ventilation elbows is an important contributor to noise in ship ventilation systems. Inspired by the leading-edge tubercles of humpback whale flippers, tubercle guide vanes are introduced to regulate the internal flow and reduce aerodynamic noise. Experimental measurements are used to validate the numerical flow and acoustic models. The effects of tubercle placement, amplitude, wavelength, and guide vane thickness are subsequently investigated. The results show that leading-edge tubercles redistribute the incoming flow before it develops along the guide vane. The redistribution suppresses local acceleration and alleviates concentrated pressure gradients near the vane entrance, thereby reducing aerodynamic noise. The geometric parameters affect the acoustic response through different flow control mechanisms. Amplitude mainly regulates the intensity of local flow redistribution. Wavelength controls its spatial extent and the interaction between adjacent tubercles. Guide vane thickness influences local flow deflection, together with the resulting velocity and pressure gradients. Effective noise reduction therefore depends on the combined adjustment of the three parameters rather than on the independent optimization of a single parameter. An orthogonal design is further employed to identify a preferred parameter combination. The optimized configuration weakens the local concentration of high-velocity flow and improves downstream pressure recovery. Lower aerodynamic noise is consequently obtained than with the conventional guide vane. The identified relationships among tubercle placement, geometric parameters, local flow regulation, and noise reduction provide a physical basis for the low-noise design of ship ventilation elbows.
title: Acoustic characteristics of a ventilation duct elbow with a whale flipper-inspired tubercle guide vane

abstract: The arcuate fasciculus (af) is a crucial dorsal pathway underpinning human language, yet its weak frontal connectivity in macaques-the standard primate model-creates an evolutionary puzzle. Here, we investigate the common marmoset, a distantly related platyrrhine with high vocal complexity, to test for convergent neural adaptations. By integrating retrograde and anterograde tracing with ultra-high-resolution diffusion MRI, we identified a robust af homolog in marmosets that is anatomically distinct from the superior longitudinal fasciculus. Comparative mapping across marmosets, macaques, chimpanzees, and humans reveals a notable similarity in connectivity patterns: The marmoset af terminates extensively in the ventrolateral frontal cortex, exhibiting a connectivity profile significantly more similar to humans than to that of the phylogenetically closer macaque. Functionally, this pathway targets cortical regions activated during vocal exchanges, partially overlapping with the human speech network. These findings suggest that the frontal connectivity of the dorsal audio-motor pathway is not strictly determined by phylogenetic proximity but represents an evolutionarily labile scaffold that undergoes lineage-specific elaboration under pressure associated with complex vocal communication.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Homologous specialization of arcuate fasciculus ventrolateral frontal connectivity in marmosets and humans

abstract: Non-human primates have long been considered to show limited flexibility in their vocal production, with changes mainly due to maturational mechanisms. However, several studies suggest that emotional, contextual and social factors are likely to affect acoustic variability in non-human primates, although it is often difficult to untangle them. In this study, we investigated whether these factors influence the acoustic variability of high whinnies, the most frequent contact call of Geoffroy’s spider monkeys (Ateles geoffroyi). We used an acoustic similarity index for each pair of high whinnies and behavioural indicators of anxiety-like emotion, context and social relationships to examine intra- and inter-individual acoustic variability. We found that anxiety-like emotion explained some acoustic variability, whereas the time two monkeys spent together did not. The main factor influencing variability was the context of emission, with high whinnies being more similar during feeding at the inter-individual level. Overall, our findings indicate a vocal convergence at the group level during feeding, possibly to enhance tolerance in a risky context.
title: Factors influencing acoustic variability in the contact calls of wild Geoffroy’s spider monkeys

abstract: Non-genuine conservation status updates threaten the trust in Red Listing, but they are necessary building blocks in science. In addition, they often highlight the critical need for basic field research. The Suweon treefrog, Dryophytes suweonensis, is a hylid species long thought to be range-restricted, and assessed as Endangered by the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species. This study aimed at determining the species of individuals encountered during call surveys in 2024 in China, and aimed to determine the areas of suitable habitat for the species. We sequenced the Cytb gene fragment and compared the acoustic properties of some individuals sampled northern China to identify the species. We also built ecological models with MaxEnt to predict suitable habitats and guide future surveys. We genetically confirmed the identity of the population as D. suweonensis, more than 985 km north of the northernmost known locality for the species. The call properties also matched with those of D. suweonensis. The ecological niche models identified a very large area with suitable habitat spanning the northern Chinese plains. The species is not endemic to the Korean Peninsula, occurring in a significantly broader range, and thus, the population size is higher than previously assumed. The species is unlikely to be threatened, and this huge range extension highlights the need for additional field surveys for all amphibian species in the area. Long term, the use of conservation prioritisation tools will highlight conservation needs in the region.
title: From threatened to widespread: a non-genuine conservation status update for a now widespread Asian Hylid

abstract: On 17 September 2024, the ICSID Tribunal in Odyssey Marine Exploration, Inc v United Mexican States (Award) (hereafter Odyssey) issued its decision related to deep seabed mining, with a particular focus on dredging permits. This case comment identifies three critical observations arising from the Award that shed light on broader debates in investment arbitration. First, the decision highlights the challenges associated with third-party interventions in investor–State dispute settlement (ISDS) proceedings, particularly in environmental matters that involve a ‘public interest’ element affecting both local communities and the environment. Second, it exposes the Tribunal’s failure to adequately situate the dispute within a broader international legal framework, including relevant principles of environmental law, ISDS jurisprudence and the law governing deep seabed mining. In this respect, the Award illustrates how future deep seabed mining disputes may generate tensions between investors and environmental protection. Third, the Award raises serious concerns regarding the risk of double recovery, demonstrating how the international investment regime may unduly empower investors3 to bring claims against States even where justice has already been served by domestic courts, or while domestic judicial proceedings remain pending. Against this background, the case comment is structured as follows: Section II provides the factual background of the dispute. Section III outlines the findings of the Majority (composed of Mr Felipe Bulnes Serrano and Dr Stanimir Alexandrov). Section IV offers reflections on the Award, including an analysis of the dissenting opinion of Professor Philippe Sands, KC. By way of analogy with the Greek mythological tale, the comment examines how the Tribunal navigated through these three critical legal issues in what may be described as a ‘lost Odyssey’. Section V concludes. The dispute began when Odyssey Marine Exploration, Inc, a firm incorporated in Nevada, United States, brought a claim against Mexico under the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA),4 with the administrative centre being ICSID, for its subsidiary incorporated in Mexico. Odyssey had been preparing for deep seabed mining activities off the coast of the Baja California Peninsula, in the Gulf of Ulloa, where it obtained a mining concession in 2012 for an area exceeding 2680 km2.5 The goal of the mining project was the exploitation of sedimentary phosphate deposits, which are vital minerals for the energy transition.6 In order for Odyssey’s Mexican subsidiary to begin deep seabed mining operations, it was required to submit an environmental impact assessment (EIA) to the relevant public authority, SEMARNAT, which is responsible for overseeing natural resources.7 Odyssey submitted two separate EIAs during the process. The first EIA was submitted but returned by SEMARNAT for further clarification regarding mitigation measures related to species and biodiversity protection, and clarification regarding technical inconsistencies.8 SEMARNAT ultimately denied permission for dredging activities, citing both environmental and technical concerns associated with deep seabed mining. The rejection decision also highlighted significant risks to five migratory species, including the endangered Caretta caretta (loggerhead sea turtle), whose survival is threatened due to their limited geographical distribution.9 Odyssey appealed this first denial to the Federal Administrative Tribunal (FAT).10 The FAT annulled SEMARNAT’s decision and criticised the agency for failing to provide adequate reasons for denying the dredging permit, particularly in relation to the five listed species.11 Subsequently, the FAT requested a reassessment of the proposal in light of additional information submitted by Odyssey as part of a second application for dredging permission. However, SEMARNAT once again rejected the request.12 This second rejection was also appealed in 2019, but by the time the Tribunal was constituted and even by the time the Award was released in September 2024, the appeal had not yet been handed down.13 Despite the ongoing appeal, Odyssey filed a claim under NAFTA, alleging a breach of the fair and equitable treatment (FET) standard due to the failure to grant the necessary dredging permission. Odyssey alleged that the rejection of permits was politically motivated and manipulated by the Secretary of SEMARNAT, Mr Pachianno, for personal and political reasons. After confirming that the FET standard under Article 1105(1) of NAFTA should be interpreted in accordance with the Interpretative Notes of the NAFTA Free Trade Commission, which are binding on any tribunal constituted under NAFTA, the Tribunal determined that the FET standard aligned with customary international law.14 Accordingly, a breach of the FET occurs if the conduct of the public authority is ‘arbitrary, grossly unfair, unjust or idiosyncratic, discriminatory, exposes the claimant to sectional or racial prejudice, or involves a lack of due process leading to an outcome which offends judicial propriety’, as stated in Waste Management v Mexico (II).15 The Majority found that the initial denial of the permit was due to personal interference by the Secretary of SEMARNAT, Mr Pachianno, who allegedly instructed SEMARNAT employees to reject the permit based on the testimony of two former employees, Mr Flores and Mr Villa, who were paid by Odyssey as witnesses—a practice not unusual in investment arbitration.16 According to the Majority, the rejection was not driven by genuine environmental concerns but by personal motives, which rendered the decision arbitrary and unfair. One of the central points of dissent by Professor Philippe Sands, KC, was his view that Mexico’s refusal to grant the permit was grounded in a broader, more holistic approach to environmental protection, rather than in narrow or purely procedural considerations (see Section IV).17 This conclusion was supported by the FAT’s first ruling, which criticised the initial rejection for lacking environmental and scientific support.18 Mr Pachianno denied the allegations.19 However, the Majority also relied on the fact that SEMARNAT publicly stated, shortly after the first rejection, that it would deny Odyssey’s renewed application for dredging activities within five days of the FAT’s ruling, thus acting arbitrarily.20 Taking all these factors into account, the Majority concluded that the denial of permits, allegedly influenced by Mr Pachianno, was attributable to Mexico, and thus constituted a breach of the FET standard under Article 1105(1) of NAFTA, even though the appeal process regarding the second rejection was still ongoing at the time.21 It is noteworthy that the Majority found a breach of the FET standard under Article 1105(1) of NAFTA, despite the fact that the Mexican judiciary had full control over the review process for the denial of permissions, as clearly demonstrated by the annulment of the first rejection decision. This approach was criticised in the dissenting opinion of Professor Philippe Sands, KC, who disagreed with the Majority’s finding that the FET standard had been breached, arguing that the actions were neither ‘shocking’ nor ‘arbitrary’.22 The Award and the dissent provide three key points of reflection, offering a critical analysis of the Majority’s decision.23 Third-party interventions may play an important role in ISDS, as they can indirectly promote environmental protection and sustainable development objectives.24 In the present case, there were two third-party interventions: one by the Center for International Environmental Law (CIEL) and another by the Sociedad Cooperativa de Producción Pesquera Puerto Chale (Cooperativa). These entities sought to present factual and legal arguments concerning the potential impacts of deep seabed mining on surrounding communities (particularly fishing communities) as well as on the marine environment in the Gulf of Ulloa.25 The Majority of the Tribunal denied permission for these third parties to intervene, stating that they had nothing to contribute to the arbitration proceedings.26 In doing so, the Majority failed to give adequate consideration to the potential role of third-party submissions,27 in providing relevant factual, legal and technical information regarding the environmental effects of deep seabed mining off the coast of the Baja California Peninsula.28 Professor Philippe Sands, KC, strongly dissented from the Majority’s decision to refuse these interventions.29 He stated that the: unique perspective [of CIEL and Cooperativa] would have been extremely valuable, and [it is] deeply regrettable that the Majority has decided that it does not wish to hear from a community that is directly affected by the outcome of the proceedings. Such a decision will only serve to undermine perceptions as the legitimacy of these proceedings.30 These interventions would have provided expert opinions explaining why Mexico refused to grant the permit for deep seabed mining, reinforcing the idea that Western or Global North companies are significant drivers of such mining activities.31 The Majority isolated the dispute at hand from environmental law more broadly by adopting a narrow view, holding that the environmental NGOs failed to demonstrate a significant interest in the dispute or that they could provide meaningful assistance to the Tribunal.32 Amici curiae have traditionally been used in matters involving public policy and public interest, such as environmental protection, public health or cultural heritage.33 Allowing amici to participate may enhance the legitimacy of arbitral proceedings.34 This is because it counterbalances the inherent logic of ISDS, which entails the confidential review of State conduct (conduct that often concerns matters of public interest), thereby limiting broader systemic accountability.35 This approach to confidentiality has also been criticised by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development.36 At the same time, the admission of prospective amici should not prejudice the outcome of the proceedings. From another perspective, as Ridi argues, amicus interventions are unlikely to succeed if the prospective amici cannot offer insights beyond those that experienced counsel could provide, a point echoed by the Majority in Odyssey.37 Ridi further observed that Odyssey illustrates a situation where the prospective amici appeared primarily to support Mexico’s position, rather than to assist the Tribunal in its deliberations.38 Even though this point is valid, the issues must also be viewed within the broader systemic context for ISDS, a regime currently facing significant challenges. In this regard, amici could serve, at least in part, to restore public trust in the system. Factually and legally, they may illuminate and remind tribunals of the broader normative framework of international law within which awards are rendered, consistent with Article 38(1)(d) of the Statute of the International Court of Justice. Admittedly, opening proceedings to public interest perspectives may prolong the process, but it would likely strengthen the perceived legitimacy of the outcome. This is essentially a question of which policy considerations should prevail. This is not to suggest that the conditions for admission as amicus curiae should be disregarded. However, the NAFTA Statement on Non-Disputing Party Participation39 includes an additional ‘public interest’40 element, which is clearly present in this case. Although tribunals retain discretion to admit amicus curiae submissions (third parties have no inherent right of participation),41 a restrictive approach in cases involving significant public interests risks overlooking the broader normative context within which ISDS operates. By excluding third-party interventions, the Tribunal missed the opportunity to consider statements and perspectives from NGOs regarding the environmental implications of deep seabed mining. An overly strict approach may prevent the Tribunal from taking into account important considerations, particularly in cases involving environmental protection. Connected to the preceding issue, a broader systemic concern arises from the narrow positioning of the case. This narrowness may be viewed as increasing the trench between international investment law and its interaction with other international legal regimes. In recent years, deep seabed mining has attracted increasing attention, particularly as activities have begun shifting from the exploration phase towards the potential extraction of critical rare earth minerals, such as ferromanganese nodules. Conversely, from the perspective of the law of the sea, States parties to the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) are under an obligation to prevent environmental harm and marine pollution, including harm arising from activities such as deep seabed mining.42 However, the Majority found that Mexico had not enacted environmental regulations per se, but rather that the rejection of permits was procedurally flawed. This raises important questions about the repercussions this case may have for future arbitration proceedings concerning deep seabed mining, specifically, whether the protection of investors will continue to prevail over the protection of the environment. These concerns are especially relevant in light of increasing calls within the deep seabed mining regime for a precautionary pause or moratorium until the Mining Code is finalised.43 Instead of prioritising investors’ rights as a starting point, the Tribunal should have placed the focus on the Gulf of Ulloa and its marine environment as the primary subject of legal protection. This view is reinforced by the fact that the Majority failed to engage with Mexico’s environmental obligations, and regrettably, Mexico itself did not advance such arguments. A nature-centred approach, guided by the precautionary principle, could have led to a different outcome.44 Similarly, by neglecting Mexico’s obligations under customary international law to preserve biodiversity and protect the environment, the Tribunal did not fully engage with the principle of systemic integration, as reflected in Article 31(3)(c) of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties (VCLT).45 Although neither disputing party expressly referred to the VCLT or to the principle of systemic integration when assessing the alleged breach of the FET standard,46 this may have constituted a missed opportunity for Mexico to invoke its customary international law obligations to protect and preserve the environment. As a result, the Tribunal may have lacked a sufficient basis to engage with this broader systemic-oriented approach to legal reasoning. Such an approach, which adjudicators ought to adopt, would have required consideration of relevant developments in international environmental law, including the significance of resolutions adopted by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) at its World Conservation Congress. These resolutions called for a moratorium on deep seabed mining exploitation, addressing its 170 Member States and more than 1400 IUCN member organisations.47 The Mexican State supported this moratorium, and yet it is now required to pay compensation. This outcome illustrates the consequences of an anthropocentric approach to international investment law, one that prioritises property rights and the interests of investors while relegating environmental considerations to a secondary position.48 Moreover, Mexico is a member of the Deep Sea Conservation Coalition, together with more than 40 States, all of which support a moratorium on deep seabed extraction until adequate mining regulations are adopted by the International Seabed Authority.49 Several of these points were raised in the third-party interventions discussed in the preceding section. This underscores the role of such interventions in illuminating the broader international legal context and reminding tribunals of their duty to operate within the wider framework of international law, particularly in light of contemporary challenges and evolving global realities. Notably, the Majority did not even refer to the VCLT, which is a missed opportunity. As such, it is a missed opportunity for the Tribunal to integrate a non-anthropocentric view into ISDS. A more integrated approach, one that acknowledged the environmental risks and potential harm posed by deep seabed mining, would have provided a more balanced and legally sound outcome, especially in light of the strong emphasis on protecting the environment in this day and age. In investment arbitration, there is a potential risk of double recovery, particularly where multiple or ongoing proceedings are taking place in the host State that may result in the State compensating the foreign investor more than once.50 This is a pressing issue and is typically raised by the respondent State. It is also relevant in the present case, as Mexico invoked this concern in light of the ongoing domestic court proceedings. As Professor Philippe Sands, KC, succinctly observed in his dissent,51 the Mexican legal system was functioning properly. One judicial body annulled the first rejection, and the second rejection remains under appeal in the Mexican courts. In the first case, justice was served. However, what happens if the second judicial decision also annuls the second rejection, even though Odyssey has already secured an international Award of US$37.1 million?52 This scenario raises significant concerns regarding double recovery, contrary to the general principle of international law enunciated in the Factory of Chorzów case, which underscored avoiding risks ‘of the same damage being compensated twice’.53 In this case, the mere risk of double compensation arising from both the Tribunal’s Award and potential domestic court proceedings is sufficient to warrant attention. Nevertheless, the issue of double recovery was addressed by the Majority.54 The Majority, however, appeared to accept uncritically the claimant investor’s submissions in their post-hearing brief,55 which relied heavily on the reasoning in Chevron v Ecuador.56 That case similarly argued that the risk of double recovery should not be because domestic a outcome for the claimant The claimant investor argued that the second rejection, which was under appeal, would to and the of a deep seabed mining permit the that the arguments of double recovery were and to a on Chevron v the that concerns regarding double recovery are not matters for international tribunals to on the or phase but should be addressed in the of a case, or after the Award has been The further v which that risks of double recovery in of proceedings should be with by domestic courts.
