abstract: Abstract Objective This study aims to address the effects of a difference in sex ratio on courtship behavior, egg production, egg hatching rate, and larval survival in Zebrafish Danio rerio, providing a theoretical basis for optimizing sex ratios in laboratory breeding conditions through systematic evaluation of the complete reproductive process from behavior to offspring viability. Methods Zebrafish broodstock (AB strain blue zebra) consisting of 15 males and 12 females (age = 7–9 months) were prepared, and two groups of fish with different sex ratios—female-biased (one male and two females [1M:2F group]) and male-biased (four males and two females [4M:2F group])—were set and allocated to breeding isolation devices for subsequent experiments. Results We compared courtship behavior, fecundity, and subsequent embryonic development. Behavioral observations showed that males in the 1M:2F group preferred a single female. The other female actively approached the male to seek stimulation, often interfering with normal courtship. In contrast, males in the 4M:2F group exhibited more intense courtship behavior, including various male–female chasing patterns, ensuring that females received sufficient stimulation. Regarding fecundity, the average egg production in the 1M:2F group was measured as 191 eggs/female, while the 4M:2F group demonstrated a mean egg count of 279 per female. Furthermore, embryonic culture showed that the 1M:2F group had a hatching rate of 28.8 ± 5.9% (mean ± SE) at 48 h, while the 4M:2F group reached 71.2 ± 8.0% at 48 h, suggesting an approximately 2.5-fold greater hatching rate for the 4M:2F group compared with the 1M:2F group. The survival rate at 72 h was 54.0 ± 18.7% for the 1M:2F group and 62.5 ± 23.5% for the 4M:2F group. Conclusions This study indicated that a male-biased sex ratio was optimal for Zebrafish reproduction in a standard Zebrafish spawning apparatus under normal spawning conditions.
title: Effects of sex ratio on courtship behavior, spawning, hatching, and larval survival in Zebrafish

abstract: Abstract Anthropogenic noise pollution induces changes in the behavior of wild animals. Birds exhibit a well-characterized response to noise pollution: by vocalizing at higher frequencies, birds can escape the masking effects of low-frequency anthropogenic sounds. Although Paris ranks among the world’s largest and most densely populated cities, in recent years Parisians have piloted a multi-faceted effort to reduce anthropogenic noise. Are the city’s noise reduction efforts sufficient to affect the frequency characteristics of city-dwelling birds? We used directional microphones to collect field recordings of Parus major (Great Tit) in noisy urban sites within Paris and quiet forest sites outside of Paris in Fontainebleau. We recorded birds at both sites during two time periods, separated by two decades, in 2003 and 2023. We collected field measurements of ambient noise using a calibrated sound level meter and we evaluated long-term noise monitoring data collected by the French government. We predicted that birds would sing higher frequency songs in noisy urban Paris compared to quiet natural areas, and we predicted that the magnitude of these differences would diminish in 2023 compared to 2003 given the city’s recent noise reduction efforts. We show that urban birds sing at higher frequencies when noise levels increase, matching previous findings from across Europe. Long term data reveal a decline in anthropogenic noise in Paris over the past decades, with average noise levels in 2023 reaching half of their previous intensity. Despite noise reduction efforts, urban birds continue to sing with higher frequencies compared to non-urban birds, and those frequencies have not declined over two decades. We conclude that the noise reduction efforts in Paris have decreased anthropogenic noise levels, but that birds maintain songs with higher minimum frequencies in spite of this change.
title: Acoustic differences persist in urban Parus major (Great Tit) over two decades of declining anthropogenic noise in Paris, France
The Road to Recovery: Using an integrated approach to recovering rapidly declining bird species, a case study with Coccyzus americanus (Yellow-billed Cuckoo)

abstract: Echolocating bats rely on precise auditory processing to navigate and forage in complete darkness. A critical aspect of this behaviour is the neural encoding of self-generated vocalizations, which allows for accurate comparison with returning echoes. In this study, we introduce a non-invasive method for recording auditory brainstem responses (ABRs) in awake, flying big brown bats (Eptesicus fuscus). Using a custom 3D-printed harness that enables sustained in-place flight, we simultaneously recorded electroencephalographic and acoustic signals from freely vocalizing animals. Self-emitted echolocation calls reliably evoked ABRs, including a distinct pre-auditory wave that occurred before call onset and is probably associated with motor command generation. We were able to extract single-trial individual ABR patterns, which revealed significant correlations between specific acoustic properties of the calls and both ABR amplitude and latency. These findings demonstrate that, despite the suggested peripheral attenuation of self-emitted echolocation calls, the bat auditory system dynamically encodes the characteristics of outgoing vocalizations, with information extraction occurring as early as the brainstem. Our approach offers an effective framework for investigating sensory-motor integration in actively behaving animals.
journal: Proceedings of the Royal Society B Biological Sciences
title: In-flight brainstem responses highlight the encoding of self-emitted echolocation calls in bats

abstract: Laughter and its associated facial expression, the play face, are critically important in the social lives of animals. Perhaps owing to this, play faces are mimicked in social interactions across many species. Despite growing interest, few works have directly compared play face mimicry across species and age groups within the same experimental framework, limiting our understanding of its developmental and evolutionary origins. In this study, we examined play face mimicry in human infants (n = 63), human adults (n = 36) and orangutans (Pongo pygmaeus; n = 6), using a tightly controlled design. We found that both human infants and adults reliably mimicked play faces, however, infants produced these robustly more than adults. Additionally, while adult humans did not produce as many play faces as infants, they produced reliably more smiles in response to the play face stimuli. When considering the orangutans, we found no evidence of play face mimicry, with only one instance observed across the entire experiment. This suggests that while our paradigm reliably induced mimicry across both human groups, our set-up may have been suboptimal to evoke mimicry responses in orangutans. This article is part of the theme issue 'Mechanisms, development, phylogeny and functions of emotional expressions'.
journal: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B Biological Sciences
title: The development of play face mimicry: comparative insights from human infants, adults and orangutans

abstract: ABSTRACT Fruit flies exhibit a complex mating ritual in which males display acoustic, visual, and/or chemical signals to increase their mating success. Females play a central role in this process by discriminating among males, evaluating them during courtship, and deciding whether to accept copulation. However, female behavior during male courtship remains poorly understood. Investigating this aspect may improve our understanding of reproductive behavior in fruit flies, revealing which behaviors benefit male mating success. The present study aimed to characterize female behaviors during male courtship and identify those associated with mating success, using three economically important fruit fly species as models: Anastrepha fraterculus (Wiedemann), Anastrepha obliqua (Macquart), and Ceratitis capitata (Wiedemann). Using video recordings, we described and analyzed the behavioral units and sequences displayed by females during male courtship. We compared the relative frequency of each behavioral unit between mated and unmated females within each species and examined differences in behavioral sequence length and duration across species. We identified 20 behavioral units in A. fraterculus , 21 in A. obliqua , and 17 in C. capitata . Behavioral patterns varied among species, with A. fraterculus and A. obliqua showing greater similarity to each other than to C. capitata , likely due to their closer phylogenetic relationship. Notably, many female behaviors mirrored those previously described in males.
title: How Do Female Pest Tephritids Behave During Male Courtship?

abstract: ABSTRACT A classic conflict of interest between the sexes occurs when males benefit from polygynous mating whereas females benefit from monopolising male parental care. In the pied flycatcher Ficedula hypoleuca , some males are polyterritorial, establishing a second territory far away from the first to attract a second female, apparently to deceive females into polygyny. Here, we focus on male song, addressing both the sender's and the receiver's perspective. We show that the individual males were singing shorter song strophes and increasing the syllable switching after they had become mated and were trying to attract a second female on a secondary territory. Thus, prospecting females may assess a male's mating status from his song. This was supported in mate choice experiments in large, outdoor aviaries where the songs from unmated and already‐mated males on secondary territories were broadcasted. The females spent most time with the male in the compartment where the song of an unmated male was broadcasted. However, this differential female response in favour of the song from an unmated male disappeared when the syllable switches of the broadcasted songs of the males were manipulated to resemble the song of a mated male. We suggest that an increased syllable switching between songs of mated males can be related to constraints of defending separate territories towards male intruders, including male neighbours and prospecting males. This is important because competition for suitable nest sites may be strong and because polyterritorial males must return frequently to the first territory to keep the nest site and the first female. Prospecting females may take advantage of the information from the song to assess male mating status and thereby avoid being deceived into polygyny.
title: Female Pied Flycatchers Ficedula hypoleuca Can Discriminate Between Songs of Unmated and Mated Males and Avoid Being Deceived Into Polygyny

abstract: Brief, loud sounds are known as impulsive noise and can trigger behavioural reactions, increase energy demand and interrupt the routine activities of organisms. However, few studies have evaluated the potential physiological costs of impulsive noise on birds under controlled conditions, hindering our understanding of its real impacts. Here, we experimentally evaluate how impulsive noise affects individual physiological and behavioural responses in Atlantic Canaries Serinus canaria . We tested the hypothesis that impulsive noise produces behavioural and physiological activation. We expected increased levels of circulating corticosterone and glucose, along with locomotor activities when canaries were exposed to simulated fireworks noise compared with background sound. Contrary to our predictions, no effect of simulated fireworks on circulating corticosterone or glucose concentrations was identified. However, when canaries were exposed to simulated fireworks, they increased the frequency of startle reflexes, jumps and calls, but decreased the number of horizontal movements on the perch and self‐grooming. We propose that birds were aware of the simulated fireworks noise and ready to react, but the stimulus did not elicit a strong physiological response under the experimental setting used in this study.
title: Simulated fireworks disrupt behaviour, but apparently not glucose or corticosterone levels in captive Atlantic canaries Serinus canaria

abstract: ABSTRACT Sound plays a central role in the lives of humpback whales ( Megaptera novaeangliae ), but elevated ambient sound levels—from either natural or anthropogenic sources—may interfere with their ability to communicate. While vocal responses to noise have been well‐documented, far less is known about how whales may adjust non‐vocal behaviors such as breaching. We investigated whether humpback whales in Glacier Bay National Park and Preserve (GBNPP), a protected foraging habitat in Southeast Alaska, modify breaching behavior in response to elevated ambient sound levels. Using a combination of long‐term acoustic monitoring and land‐based visual surveys conducted over two humpback whale foraging seasons (2015–2016), we assessed breaching occurrence and frequency in relation to measured ambient sound. We found that higher ambient sound levels were significantly associated with an increased likelihood of breaching and a greater number of breaches per observation period. Notably, this effect was driven by total ambient sound level, not by the presence or proximity of vessels, suggesting that whales respond to acoustic sources equally in this system. Our results support the hypothesis that breaching may function as a compensatory communication strategy when vocal signals are masked, and that this strategy is transferable between sound sources. Our findings underscore the importance of managing ambient sound in sensitive habitats and suggest that low‐noise protected areas like GBNPP may buffer whales from more disruptive effects of ocean noise.
title: The Effect of Ambient Noise on Humpback Whale Breaching Behavior on a Southeast Alaskan Foraging Ground

abstract: ABSTRACT Harbor porpoises ( Phocoena phocoena ) are among the most widespread cetacean species in Irish waters and are listed under Annex II of the EU Habitats Directive as a species of community importance. The local harbor porpoise population in Dublin Bay coexists with designated spoil grounds for dredging activity, which has increased due to Dublin Port's Alexandra Basin Redevelopment (ABR) project. This study examines the long‐ and short‐term effects of dredge disposal on harbor porpoise foraging behavior over a 5‐year period (2017–2021). Acoustic monitoring using C‐PODs was conducted inside and outside the Burford Bank disposal site. The effect of dredge disposal on foraging intensity (quantified by hourly buzz:click ratio) was analyzed using Generalized Additive Mixed Models (GAMMs) and assessed using modified Before–After (BA) and Before–After Control‐Impact (BACI) frameworks. We classified 33% of detected clicks as buzzes. Foraging intensity increased during three of the four dredging phases compared to non‐dredging periods at all monitored locations, including the control site. Short‐term responses, however, were highly site‐specific. These findings suggest that dredge disposal had no obvious negative impact on harbor porpoise foraging behavior and may have increased food availability. This study provides valuable insights into balancing species conservation with infrastructure development.
title: Harbor Porpoises ( Phocoena phocoena ) in Dublin Bay: How Does Dredge Disposal Affect Foraging Behavior?

abstract: Underwater sound is crucial for cetaceans, aiding behaviors such as foraging, communication, navigation, and reproduction. The St. Lawrence Estuary (eastern Canada), a key habitat for several cetacean species, also serves as a major shipping corridor connecting the Great Lakes to the Atlantic Ocean, which exposes marine mammals to elevated levels of anthropogenic noise. Given the threatened status of species such as the blue whale (Balaenoptera musculus) and the beluga whale (Delphinapterus leucas), quantifying underwater noise and identifying its sources is essential for effective conservation. This study, conducted within the framework of the MARS (Marine Acoustic Research Station) project, analyzes acoustic data recorded from August to October 2021 in the Laurentian Channel. A model was developed to classify and quantify wind- and shipping traffic-generated noise across three biologically relevant frequency bands: 50, 300, and 6300 Hz. Results show that at 50 Hz, used by blue whales, traffic noise dominates nearly 100% of the time. At 6300 Hz, used by belugas, traffic noise accounts for 24.4% of the measured levels. These findings emphasize the importance of frequency- and species-specific assessments to inform mitigation strategies and support the development of sustainable marine traffic policies.
journal: The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America
title: Wind-dependent and traffic-generated noise in marine mammal habitat: Assessment across three frequency bands in the St. Lawrence estuary

abstract: Whistles play an important role in communication among dolphins. Although whistles of rough-toothed dolphins (Steno bredanensis) have been investigated elsewhere, no information is available in the South China Sea. Using acoustic recordings collected during confirmed visual sightings, this study provides the first detailed description of whistle characteristics from two groups of rough-toothed dolphins in the South China Sea and compares them with those of the same species in other regions. A total of 267 whistles were extracted from 79 min of recording from two groups across two encounters, with fundamental frequencies ranged from 2.09 to 16.20 kHz. Upsweep (38.20%) were the most frequent contours, and two stereotyped whistles were identified. Further, three types of nonlinear features were observed on some of the recorded whistles, including steps, side bands, and deterministic chaos. This study is the first to describe the whistles of rough-toothed dolphins in the South China Sea with results indicating that whistles of this population differ in contour composition and acoustic parameters from those of other conspecific populations. These findings provide valuable insights into the whistles of rough-toothed dolphins and will further provide baseline data for the detection and identification of rough-toothed dolphins through passive acoustic monitoring.
journal: The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America
title: Whistle characteristics of free-ranging rough-toothed dolphins ( Steno bredanensis ) in the South China Sea

abstract: Since first being scientifically recognised almost 150 years ago, bowhead whale (Balaena mysticetus) song has been documented as a remarkably diverse form of communication. While songs in other taxa play fundamental roles in sexual selection and social organisation, the function of bowhead whale song remains poorly understood, in part due to a lack of studies that quantifiably explore variation in song and its fine-scale structure. Here, variation in the songs of Bering-Chukchi-Beaufort bowhead whales was quantified across three years (2011, 2014, 2020) using unit-level analyses and similarity metrics (Levenshtein distance and Dice's similarity). In each year, songs formed distinct song types, some of which remained stable for several weeks, while others changed rapidly within minutes. This variation was uneven across song components, revealing that songs contain a combination of persistent and variable features. By showing that stability and plasticity co-occur in an acoustic display, these findings indicate that multiple, possibly interacting selective pressures, including ecological constraints, social organisation, and sexual selection, may shape song structure. Overall, this study introduces a reproducible framework for song analysis, which provides a foundation for the cross-year and cross-population comparisons essential in understanding the role and evolution of bowhead whale songs.
journal: The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America
title: Fine-scale quantitative analysis of bowhead whale ( Balaena mysticetus ) song shows varying stability of song types

abstract: While many studies have demonstrated the negative impacts of anthropogenic noise on aquatic animals, few studies have examined its effect on species that inhabit major ports. New York City provides habitat for the oyster toadfish (Opsanus tau), a species in which females must hear the male advertisement call to reproduce. This study had two equally important goals. First, vessel noise in the waters of New York City was characterized: An analysis of 480 vessel noise events revealed that noise incidence varied widely, while amplitude varied less. Second, toadfish calling behavior was quantified under noisy and quiet conditions. Toadfish called over twice as much in quiet samples, which occurred in the early morning, than in samples with noise. This early morning peak in calling behavior differs from those of non-urban populations and is evidence of diurnal call suppression. Furthermore, in samples with noise, toadfish actively called less when noise duration was longer, amplitude was greater, and the dominant frequency of noise overlapped the fundamental frequency of calls. Finally, toadfish did not change call amplitude, frequency or duration during noise. These results provide evidence that fishes living in vessel-heavy urban environments adjust their reproductive-related acoustic communication behavior to cope with noise.
journal: The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America
title: The oyster toadfish ( Opsanus tau ) alters active and diurnal calling amid vessel noise in New York City

abstract: The wideband ambiguity function (WAF) is a foundational tool for analyzing sonar signals, as it jointly characterizes time delay and Doppler-induced time stretching. However, when applied to nonstationary biological signals, this function is sensitive to temporal misalignment and integration-window effects, which can bias estimates of sonar performance. This paper proposes a corrected formulation of the WAF that compensates for Doppler-induced temporal shifts by centering the analysis around the energy centroid of the emitted signal. The corrected wideband ambiguity function (CWAF) preserves the intrinsic resolution properties imposed by signal bandwidth and duration, while ensuring invariance to time translation and integration time within the analysis window. This method is applied to field recordings of echolocation during foraging and depredation, produced by bats (Pipistrellus kuhlii) and sperm whales (Physeter macrocephalus). The results reveal contrasting biosonar strategies: bats dynamically modulate spectral and temporal parameters across foraging phases, whereas sperm whales emit spectrally stable, Doppler tolerant pulses and primarily adjust inter-click intervals and output levels. Additionally, analyzing the resolution of pulses P0 and P1 lends support to the hypothesis of a three-dimensional sperm whale biosonar model. Overall, the CWAF provides a robust framework for linking biosonar signal design, estimator theory, and animal behavior.
journal: The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America
title: A corrected wideband ambiguity function for robust biosonar strategy analysis

abstract: American bullfrogs pose a significant threat to local biodiversity in regions where they are non-native, as they spread diseases and prey on smaller species. Therefore, being able to monitor their population changes in local habitats is important for effective policymaking and conservation efforts. This study investigates the use of a single passive acoustic sensor, AudioMoth, to estimate the number of vocal bullfrogs in natural habitats. Several noise removal methods are applied to the spectrograms of audio recordings, after which spectral features of bullfrog calls are extracted and analyzed using a spectral clustering method. Calls are grouped into clusters, with the number of clusters corresponding to the estimated number of vocal bullfrogs in the dataset. The proposed method demonstrated close agreement with field observations, achieving a mean absolute error of 0.85 across 13 field observation cases at seven ponds in 2023. In a complementary 2024 dataset, results were consistent with estimates derived from an acoustic localization approach using an array of Global Positioning System-synchronized AudioMoth sensors. These results indicate the feasibility of estimating numbers of vocal bullfrogs using passive acoustic data from a single sensor. The proposed method can be extended to other species, provided the spectral structure of individual calls exhibits differences.
journal: The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America
title: Estimating the number of vocal bullfrogs using a single passive acoustic sensor

abstract: There is mounting evidence from many species that physiological state can be reflected in external cues, such as the structure of vocalizations. North American red squirrels ( Tamiasciurus hudsonicus (Erxleben, 1777)) produce individually distinct territorial vocalizations, called rattles, containing information relating to both a proximate stressor and reproductive condition. Given the importance of these vocalizations in communicating territory ownership, and their ability to contain cues relating to physiological state, we hypothesized that information regarding individual circulating glucocorticoid concentrations is transmitted between conspecifics within an audible range. We analysed fecal cortisol metabolite (FCM) concentrations from 129 red squirrels, comparing focal individual FCMs to conspecific FCMs within an acoustic neighbourhood. We found support for our hypothesis through a significant positive relationship between the FCM concentrations of focal squirrels and their neighbours independent of local density. These findings demonstrate that individual physiology interacts with conspecific physiology at ecologically relevant spatial scales and suggest that the social relationships between individual red squirrels may play a larger role in dictating individual responses to the environment.
title: Individual physiological state is influenced by the physiological state of conspecifics within red squirrel acoustic neighbourhoods

abstract: Throughout West Africa’s Cross River basin, regional identities developed in recent centuries through trade exchanges among small forest-dwelling communities, from the foothills of the Bamenda Highlands to the port of Calabar (Fig. 1). In the process, the Ékpè “leopard” society was established as the community police of the region, each “principality” having its own lodge (Miller 2009; Miller and Ojong 2012).2 At the top of the food chain, the leopard served as metaphor for the ideal consciousness of a council of titleholders, whose collective decisions were the final say in community matters. Like the solitary leopard, Ékpè titleholders were expected to be cautious and observant to detect antisocial behavior, and to pounce rapidly in resolving problems through council decisions.Elephants also served as metaphors for leadership; described as “monsters of the land,” they represented an awesome power within the forest.3 Since elephants move in herds, lineage heads displayed their tusks as a symbol of their ability to unify their people. Carved elephant tusk horns signaled paternal authority; elephant tail hairs inserted into caps identified lineage leadership, and elephant images performed in communal rites emphasized the immensity of a ritual investiture. In all cases, these symbols used in ceremony informed local deities and ancestors that a consecrated lineage head was requesting their support on behalf of the community.The leopard, elephant, and other animals are believed to have a spiritual avatar. These “mystic” animals participate in royal investitures and proclamations: Ékpè initiations are authorized through the resounding “voice of the leopard,” while important events are proclaimed when a tusk trumpet is blown to produce “the voice of the elephant.”4 These reverberations alert the entire community, which includes the living, the deities of the territory under their jurisdiction, and the ancestors buried there, as in the example from Úrúán in Figure 2.5Available evidence suggests that in the distant past these symbols emerged as totems for migrating kin-groups or lineages. Lévi-Strauss linked totemism to regimes of hunting/gathering or “shifting cultivation,” where foraging terrain and/or gardening plots rotate every few years and the residence adapts accordingly.6 In the Upper Cross River, Idoma prehistory of the sixteenth-nineteenth centuries fits this template: “The examination of totems has emerged as one of the new methodological devices for the historian of pre-colonial Africa” (Erim 1978: 56, following Webster 1975). Kindreds were differentiated from each other by observing “an iho (an animal forbiddance)”; for example: “all the kindred groups which observe the ogonopo fish totem are descended from a common ancestor, Ode,” even if they became geographically scattered (Erim 1978: 61).Early twentieth century reports by British colonists in the Calabar region contain garbled hints of totemic organization, which Amaury Talbot perceived as the historical origin of a regional club7:When settlements became permanent and fostered heritable land claims, totems were repurposed as political symbols as in regional multiethnic institutions like Ékpè and the Njoku Malé “elephant medicine” society, described below.8As Old Calabar became a major Atlantic port through contact with European traders, captive humans, elephant tusks, and other forest products were dispersed across the Atlantic world. Carved elephant tusks that entered Europe from the 1500s onwards are maintained in museum collections. In the Calabar region elephant tusks are inherited as royal property within lineages, while in the Caribbean the Cuban descendants of Africans maintain elephant and leopard symbols within initiation lineages as emblematic of their African heritage, specifically the Ocha and Ifá systems of the Lukumí (Yorùbá) and Arará (Fon) as well as the Abakuá mutual aid society derived from the Ékpè institution of the Cross River region, as discussed below.9Both the African Forest Elephant (Loxodonta cyclotis) and Leopard (Panthera pardus) are native to the entire forest belt of Atlantic Africa (from Senegal to Angola).10 The earliest evidence of elephants and leopards as royal symbols in southeastern Nigeria was dated to the ninth century; southeast of Onitcha, the Ìgbò Úkwú royal burial site included three ivory tusks, as well as bronze pendants of an elephant head, a leopard’s head, and a shell surmounted by a leopard (Shaw 1973: 18; 1970: 68, fig. 14).Portuguese merchant navigators visiting the Gulf of Guinea brought elephant tusks into Europe in the 1500s, and cartographers began to identify Africa with elephants.11 A map produced in 1636 in Amsterdam shows elephants in “Biafara” (later called “Biafra”), which includes the Cross River region (Fig. 3).Early traffickers referred to captive Africans as “black ivories,” while trading firearms, gunpowder, alcohol, and textiles for ivory tusks and humans (Ardener 2001: 128, 130.) An elephant with a howdah is central to the coat of arms of the Royal African Company, established in 1660 by London merchants.12 Both ivories and humans were documented in trade reports from the Calabar region by D.P. Pereira (Portuguese, 1506), O. Dapper (Dutch, 1668), and J. Barbot (French, 1678 onwards):As African ivories and captive Africans entered Lisbon, by 1550, 10% of the population of Lisbon and other towns were West and Central Africans (Saunders 1982: xi, 7, 13, 15-16, 20-21, 54-55).13 Shipping records document trade in ivories and humans over the centuries: for example, the French ship La Pourvoyance, laden with a cargo of slaves and 500 pounds of ivory, was captured in 1793 by John Tobin of Liverpool, master of the privateer Gipsy (Latham (1974: 863). The exchange of enslaved people for “36 Elephants Teeth” was documented in the 1784 voyage of the Golden Age from Badagry to Jamaica (Lovejoy 2018: 47).14 Some ivory entered the Caribbean, as an 1835 Havana court case documented an African cabildo “nation group” in possession of “a piece of elephant tusk with two faces engraved in it [that] serves as a small bell to call to God” (Lovejoy 2018: 91). Elephant and even leopard ivory has ever remained an important heritage symbol for Afro-Caribbean people, as we will see.Carved elephant ivory horns in European collections were identified by Ezio Bassani as arriving from “1551-1600.” He concluded they were from the Calabar region, and “carved in one workshop … between the end of the sixteenth and the middle of the seventeenth centuries” (Bassani 2000: 266).15 Bassani based his analysis on carving styles and symbols, mainly crocodile or tortoise forms used today on the coded ùkárá cloth used in the Ékpè “leopard” society (see Fig. 13).16 These symbols were also carved into elephant tusks in the Grassfields region of Cameroon, as Chris Geary observed: “In design, these tusks [display] … icons common in the Grassfields repertoire… . the outer bands of rainbow lizard and elephant allude to royal power …” (Geary 1992: 235). Locals view the animals displayed on the royal cloth and tusks of this region as messengers of the deities that support the investiture of lineage heads.Having summarized the known history of elephant tusk and leopard symbols in Calabar and its hinterlands, the following presents the author’s research findings in several communities that display them in rites and royal dress.From Benin City to the west and the Cross River region to the east, both elephant and leopard symbols are displayed in contemporary royal procedures (Fig. 4). The ubiquity of ivory sumptuary goods across the West African forest zone, including bracelets, anklets, and trumpets as well as tusks on ancestral shrines, bespeaks their central role as signs of wealth, privilege, and political authority. Some of these uses were also tied to ritualized hunting, symbolizing the prestige of preagricultural social organization and its importance in many local institutions of chieftaincy. The nearly total recent disappearance of elephant and leopard populations across the region renders this powerful ecological-political prehistory less visible to outside visitors, but it remains vivid in folk memory and visible in sumptuary regalia as in these examples.The Bangwa of Fontem, Cameroon, were a trade link between the Cross River region and the Grasslands. Robert Brain learned in the 1960s that Bangwa “patrilineal as well as matrilineal ancestors are worshipped through their successors who are the custodians of the ancestral skulls” (Brain 1972: 107).In Fontem in the early twenty-first century, elephant and leopard symbols were paramount during the investiture of a village head as an Ékpè titleholder. After his training and consecration by elders in the nearby sacred forest grove, the village head led several processions from the grove to his compound; the third featured a mobile “house” representing a “spiritual elephant” draped in the ndop cloth of the Grassfields region (Fig. 5).17This village head, Mr. Philip Tazi (a.k.a. Sisiku Mbe Tazi Ate’awung IX) describes the third procession:Elephant hair caps are a corresponding royal symbol used by lineage heads. Their use extends to Bangwa and Manyu in Cameroon and to Éjághám-speaking communities in eastern Nigeria (“Ekoi” on colonial maps; for details see Geary 1992: 230 figs. 11–13, and Notué and Triaca 2005: 178). In Íkóm, a Clan Head wears an inherited elephant hair cap (Fig. 6). In the same community, the façade of an Ékpè hall displays a painted elephant (Fig. 7).Among Ngóló-speaking people in South West Cameroon, a village council consulted the oracle before commencing an Ékpè event, which responded positively. In response, the overall head of local traditional societies blew an inherited elephant tusk horn—which he claimed to be centuries old—to herald the blessing of the ancestors and deities of the land. (Fig. 8).21After this affirmation, an Njoku Malé “elephant medicine” mask emerged from the forest through a spiritually protective gateway (Fig. 9), then moved throughout the village to purify the space (Fig. 10), and finally entered the Ékpè hall (Fig. 11). Njoku Malé is a royal initiation club represented by body-masks. Edwin Ardener reported:Indigo-dyed ùkárá cloth is used exclusively by Ékpè society members. Eli Bentor documented ùkárá cloths made by contractors from Arochukwu communities, while Ábíríbá (phonetic spelling “Ébíríbá”) locals also claim that workshops operated in their communities (Fig. 12) (Bentor 2015).23 Produced in Ábíríbá decades ago, a rare cloth portrays an elephant, leopard, frog, turtle, crayfish, and crab as messengers of the deities of the land and water evoked by Ékpè initiates (Fig. 13).24 Another rare example featuring an elephant form was used as the backdrop for a Clan Head’s throne in Calabar (Fig. 14).Among the Yakurr people of Ugep, each head of a paternal family possesses an elephant tusk horn. During important events, a family head will appear holding a staff while his assistant blows an elephant tusk horn (Fig. 15).25 From this community, Dr. Otu Abam Ubi explains:In the port city of Calabar, Èfịk-speaking clans are organized into a dozen houses, derived from the trading “canoe-houses” of the seventeenth through nineteenth centuries (Dike 1956: 34; Miller 2009: 76). During annual celebrations, Cobham House is represented by banner featuring a portrait of founding ancestor Éyọ Émà on a throne, wearing a leopard-skin headband with an ivory tusk under each foot (Fig. 16). Èfịk Houses are proud of their centuries of contact with British merchants, reflected in the name Cobham, an anglicized variant of Akabom.27In the same annual celebration, each Èfịk house displayed a representative mask. A crowd-pleaser was the raffia-fiber Íbóm mask with a long “elephant trunk” and two short tusks (Fig. 17). Although Íbóm is not part of the Ékpè society, only Ékpè initiates may act as Íbóm participants, who perform songs and rhythms of the yàkpè Ékpè grade.28 Íbóm performance once again emphasizes interplay between leopard and elephant symbols.Calabar author Bassey Efiong Bassey reported that “an elephant represents Oku Akama,” alluding to the early functions of this Ékpè grade to knock down the thatched dwellings of those who resisted decisions of the council of elders.29 He describes this Ékpè grade as “well equipped for demolition …. Oku Akama is animalistic in form. The Elephant and her baby represent it. This is aptly demonstrated in its dance form” (Fig. 18) (Bassey 2001: 67, 119).30Among the Èfịks of Calabar, Èfé Àsàsbọ (hall of the python), is an Ńdèm shrine where the Èdídèm (sovereign) is invested (Goldie [1862] 1964: 601).31 A selected Ètúbòm “head of House” is first invested here as Èdídèm before receiving a government certificate making him the Obong of Calabar, “the single being who more than any other man united in himself the quintessence and grandeur and, perhaps, sanctity of the Efik tradition” (Hart 1964: 5).32 An enthroned Èdídèm was photographed in 1973 outside the Èfé Àsàsbò with each foot placed upon a nuk-enen “elephant tusk” (Fig. 19).33Calabar indigenes are organized into three historically distinct communities, Èfịk, Efût, and Qua. The secretary of Big Qua Clan, “Èsínjò Ótóè” Èdím Íká Èdím Ìtákpô, spoke about elephant symbols in royal processions of his community (Fig. 20)34:The recent Ndidem (Paramount Ruler and Éjághám Patriarch) of the Quas of Calabar, Patrick I. Oquagbor V, reflected about the leopard skin cap and elephant tusk symbols of his throne:Contemporary royal displays of elephant and leopard symbols derive from a precolonial context irrevocably altered through early trade with Europeans who brought firearms, subsequent colonial administrations that transformed the societies, leading to the widespread loss of local languages, along with destruction of the forest environment. These tragedies are reflected in the transformation of leopard symbols, for example in urban Calabar, where some Ékpè titleholders now claim that ékpè/mgbè means “lion,” and not “leopard,” as established in the historical literature.36 This transformation was visualized in a painting on the Ékpè hall of Ekondo Titi community in Cameroon, known locally as Etana or Mátámò (Fig. 21).37 Here, the painted seal of an Ékpè hall features the symbol of a lion, thus erasing a centuries long tradition of identification with the native Panthera pardus.The contemporary symbol of a lion vs. a leopard indicates several factors: a West African population disconnected from the critically endangered wildlife of their region, the inconsistent translation of local terms into Nigerian Pidgin, the loss of literacy in local languages, and perhaps the persistent prominence of the lion as symbol of British monarchy, as presented on the royal coat of arms of the United Kingdom from 1837 onwards.38In Cuba, the Abakuá mutual aid society—established in Havana in the early 1800s as a variant of Cross River’s Ékpè institution—ritually reproduces “the Voice of the leopard,” while an Abakuá visual arts tradition frequently reproduces leopard images.39 Elephant images and even carved ivory arrived to Cuba in tandem with human trafficking. One Abakuá manuscript reports about West African ivory merchants: “Batanga: Dealer (of petty merchandise and ivory)”—which is corroborated by the diary of Thomas Hutchinson, a British visitor to Batanga (present Kribi, Cameroon) in the late 1850s (Cabrera 2020: 76, 409n71).40 Several Abakuá references to elephants in regards to founding rites in West Africa were documented by folklorist Lydia Cabrera.41 Initiated elders taught her that “in the beginning,” ritual offerings included ivory: “Some spells are done with animal teeth, from mokueriré ndó (elephant), from ngrí (tiger), and also with the teeth of deceased humans” (Cabrera 1988a: 246).42In the 1800s in Havana, an ivory horn was sounded by an Arará (Fon) cabildo “nation group” during funerals and annual processions “celebrated on the day of Easter Pentecost,” exemplifying how Africans adapted their heritage practices to the Cuban context, as reported by Cuban scholar Fernando Ortiz (1955: 334-35).Another West African system recreated in colonial Cuba was Ifá divination. The Ifá oracle sign “Obe Kana” contains a parable of how Orula (deity of divination) used the elephant tusk.43 Lydia Cabrera published a literary version of this legend44:In both West Africa and Cuba, the irọfa or irọke “oracle tapper” is made in the shape of an elephant tusk, while the myth of Ifá’s foundation in West Africa narrates that all parts of the elephant were used.45 Some contemporary Cuban babaláwos possess ivory “oracle tappers” produced in West Africa and gifted from colleagues there (Fig. 22). Elephants are symbols of both Ifá divination and “Òrìṣà funfun” (white deities), specifically Ọbàtálá (Bascom (1969/1991: 185n3).46 In Havana in the decade of 1950, Ortiz reported trumpet made of … among the of the in the of a of the used in ceremony are with that the An elephant in the context of other Ifá oracle symbols was featured on one (Fig. in Havana for and Abakuá this presents the Ifá oracle as an of West African royal the Cross River during the precolonial and other animals appear to have totems for early migrating From the once permanent settlements were established for of the region, the lineage totems their functions to symbols for regional initiation led by royal members. abstract: Cross-culturally, the evolution and production of color words has been linked to communicative efficiency. In visual search tasks for instance, speakers will direct a listener to a target by referring to both its color and shape even when all the targets are unique. Moreover, speakers produce these redundant color adjectives more in languages where they precede the noun, like English, than in ones where they are postnominal, like Spanish. These results are consistent with an Incremental Collaborative Efficiency Hypothesis: the proposal that speakers are sensitive to listeners' online processing demands. If this is the case, speakers should be especially likely to produce redundant color adjectives for children, since children's visual search is especially slow. Here we show that English (Experiment 1) and Spanish-speaking (Experiment 2) adults, and parents and non-parents alike (Experiment 3), selectively generate redundant color adjectives for children. This is not because of a general bias towards being over-informative with children: when redundant color adjectives are uninformative and would not promote efficient search, speakers are no more likely to use them with children than adults (Experiment 4). Finally, children's own use of redundant color adjectives for efficient communication changes over development. Four to ten-year-olds are less likely to produce redundant color adjectives than adults but nonetheless do so selectively when addressing younger children (Experiments 5 and 6). Collectively, these results suggest that sensitivity to listeners' online processing demands is robust, emerges relatively early in development, and may especially benefit young learners.
title: Brown Bear, Brown Bear, What Do You See? Speakers Use More Redundant Color Adjectives When Speaking to Children Than Adults

abstract: This research investigates how the soundscape of Native forests reflects forest health and how it may signal early signs of Kauri Mate ( Phytophthora agathidicida ; dieback) infection. Grounded in mātauranga Māori (Māori [the Indigenous peoples of New Zealand] knowledge) from Te Rarawa (a tribe in the northern North Island, New Zealand), the study combines Indigenous knowledge with modern technology to develop a sonic-based method for ecological restoration. Recorded soundscapes from healthy kauri (a coniferous tree, northern New Zealand; Agathis australis ) are layered with taonga puoro (traditional Māori instruments), karakia (chants), and parāoa (sperm whale) calls, blended with the 528 Hz healing frequency to create immersive environments aligned with the forest’s mauri (life force). This methodology acknowledges the interconnectedness of all living entities and aims to restore ecosystems through vibration and sound. Findings recommend community-led, culturally grounded soundscape interventions to support forest health, while strengthening spiritual and emotional connections between people, place, and environment.
journal: AlterNative An International Journal of Indigenous Peoples
title: Ihirangaranga: interwoven tapestry of connection through vibration and frequencies

abstract: ECR Spotlight is a series of interviews with early-career authors from a selection of papers published in Journal of Experimental Biology and aims to promote not only the diversity of early-career researchers (ECRs) working in experimental biology but also the huge variety of animals and physiological systems that are essential for the ‘comparative’ approach. Shizuki Nara is an author on ‘ Tactile pup loss and acoustic signal enhance selective maternal retrieval behavior in echolocating bats, Pipistrellus abramus’, published in JEB. Shizuki conducted the research described in this article while a master's student in Shizuko Hiryu and Kohta I Kobayasi's lab at the Graduate School of Life and Medical Sciences, Doshisha University, Japan, where she investigated the acoustic and tactile cues that trigger maternal behavior in the Japanese house bat (Pipistrellus abramus). Shizuki is now a software engineer.
title: ECR Spotlight – Shizuki Nara

abstract: Background Passive acoustic monitoring (PAM) combined with deep learning is increasingly used to detect cetacean vocalizations. The workflow from raw audio to a trained detector (annotation, segmentation, spectrogram parameterization, image processing, and model evaluation) is rarely documented in sufficient detail to allow other groups to reproduce or compare results. This lack of standardization limits methodological comparability across studies and hinders systematic investigation of how upstream preprocessing choices affect detection performance. Methods This article presents ai-pam-pipeline, an open-source six-stage framework that formalizes the complete CNN-based detection workflow, with every parameter defined in a single YAML configuration file ensuring exact experimental reproducibility. The framework separates the methodological structure from its computational implementation, allowing adaptation to different species, vocalization types, or acoustic environments, through configuration alone, without code modification. Validation was conducted on recordings of bottlenose dolphin (Tursiops truncatus) whistles through two complementary experiments: (A) a binary whistle detector trained with controlled environment recordings, and evaluated on an independent open-ocean dataset, and (B) a five-class vocalization classifier demonstrating framework scalability. Results The binary detector achieved macro F1 = 0.966 under ten-folds cross-validation on in-domain data. Cross-domain evaluation produced zero false positives across all ten folds (false discovery rate = 0.000) with macro F1 = 0.759, confirming generalization to unseen acoustic conditions without retraining. The multiclass extension achieved macro F1 = 0.843 across five vocalization categories; inter-class confusion between echolocation click trains and burst-pulse sounds reflects biological signal overlap rather than classifier failure. Conclusions The framework provides a reproducible and documented baseline for CNN-based cetacean detection in PAM. The complete toolkit is publicly released under the Apache 2.0 license, while the datasets used in this study are made openly available through separate public repositories. Together, these resources enable exact replication of the analyses and support adaptation to new monitoring contexts.
title: An open reproducible framework for CNN-based cetacean vocalization detection in passive acoustic monitoring

abstract: Angiogenesis is essential for normal embryonic development and contributes to the progression of many angiogenesis-dependent diseases. Although several Cinnamomum species possess antiangiogenic properties, the biological activity of the Philippine endemic Cinnamomum rupestre remains poorly understood. This study evaluated the embryotoxic and antiangiogenic effects of aqueous bark decoction of C. rupestre using the mallard duck (Anas platyrhynchos) chorioallantoic membrane (CAM) assay. Fertilized duck eggs were assigned to an untreated control, solvent control (double-distilled water), positive control (retinoic acid), and five extract concentrations (6.25%, 12.5%, 25%, 50%, and 100%). Embryos were harvested on day 17 for morphometric measurements (crown-to-rump, forelimb, hindlimb, and beak lengths), while antiangiogenic activity was quantified by fractal dimension index (FDI) analysis of CAM vascular images using ImageJ. Morphometric data were analyzed using one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s HSD test. All morphometric parameters were significantly affected by treatment (p< 0.001). Embryos exposed to the 100% extract exhibited the shortest crown-to-rump, forelimb, and beak lengths, whereas lower concentrations were generally comparable with the controls. CAM vascular complexity declined significantly with increasing extract concentration (F(6,28) = 22.98, p< 0.0001; η² = 0.831), and the undiluted extract reduced FDI by approximately 29.5% relative to the untreated control. Complete embryo mortality in the retinoic acid group confirmed assay sensitivity. These findings provide the first experimental evidence that aqueous bark decoction of C. rupestre exhibits concentration-dependent embryotoxic and antiangiogenic activities, supporting its potential as a source of bioactive compounds for future phytochemical and molecular investigations.
title: Antiangiogenic potential and embryotoxicity of the aqueous bark extract of the endemic Philippine Cinnamon (Cinnamomum rupestre) in mallard duck embryos using the chorioallantoic membrane assay
